paper_title: Periscope: Extending Frozen Language Models Beyond Their Context Window

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A language model reads long text in one quadratic forward pass, stops at the context window, and loses accuracy with length before reaching it. We ask whether the read can be factorized when deciding over a finite set: which document is relevant, which option is supported, which passage is the evidence. Periscope, a training-free inference method, arranges the $N$ chunks of a text on a $K{\times}K$ grid with $K{=}\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil$ and asks a frozen model the same question about $K$ local spans of consecutive chunks and $K$ strided spans that sample the whole text, reading the log-odds of every answer at one token. Each answer takes its best local and strided score, and scoring every chunk by its two spans gives an evidence map at no further cost, whose peak is the chunk behind the answer. Every probe is about $\sqrt{sc}$ tokens for a text of $s$ tokens and chunk size $c$, so a window of $W$ tokens reaches $W^{2}/c$ tokens at $s^{1.5}$ cost. The map replaces the long read. On LongBench v2, reading only the $K$ chunks the map ranks highest, 9k tokens, matches the same model's best window read across windows from 32k to 1M tokens, and on InfiniteBench, where the median context is 150k tokens, it leads the best window read by 5 points. The same map ranks BRIGHT's long-document corpora with the best NDCG@10 of six methods. Each call caches only one probe, so a 27B model reads 4.5M-token contexts on one 80GB GPU, where a single pass would need 296GB of cache. A long read then needs a GPU that holds the model, not one that holds the text.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A language model reads long text in single forward pass, and the pass has three limits. Its attention cost grows with the square of the input. It stops at the context window. And it loses accuracy before it gets there: most long-context models fall below quality threshold well before their claimed length (Hsieh et al., 2024), 11 of 13 models claiming 128k tokens fall below half of their short-context accuracy by 32k once the needle shares little vocabulary with the question (Modarressi et al., 2025), and accuracy drops with input length even when every relevant passage is present (Du et al., 2025). Three responses exist, each with structural limit. Extending the window (Peng et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024) moves the wall and keeps the quadratic cost and the monolithic memory of the pass. Reading less, by retrieving chunks with an embedding model (Karpukhin et al., 2020) or compressing the prompt (Jiang et al., 2023), lets another model decide what enters the pass, with no guarantee that what it kept is what the question needs. Reading in pieces bounds every call, but passage scoring sees each piece alone (Dai & Callan, 2019) and chain of agents passes lossy summary from one piece to the next (Zhang et al., 2024b), so nothing relates the final answer to read of the whole text. We start from what the read is for. Many long-context reads are decisions over finite set: which document is relevant, which option is supported, which passage is the evidence. Such decision needs only one supporting passage. Mainly, document is relevant if some parts of it support the query, and an option is correct if some passage establishes it. frozen model can judge, from bounded window, whether that window supports an answer, and the bounded window is also where the model is accurate. So the text can be covered by bounded windows and the answers composed by maximum, which adds no approximation of its own, and the answer distribution over the windows is an estimate of where the evidence sits. Periscope (Figure 2) is that read: an inference method with which frozen model served at window of tokens reads texts of up to 2/c tokens, for chunk size c, with memory bounded per call. It uses the same forward pass and the same one-token readout as the single read, applied to bounded inputs, with nothing generated, no state between calls, and no orchestration. The chunks of text . The model answers the same question about local are arranged on KK grid with K= spans, each of consecutive chunks, and strided spans, each joining every K-th chunk so that it samples the whole text. Every chunk is read twice by 2K independent calls of about sc tokens for text of tokens, at cost growing as s1.5. Each answer takes its best local and its best strided score, and scoring every chunk by the two spans it lies in gives map of where the evidence sits, whose peak is the chunk behind the answer. The same map serves every task through fixed readout: it ranks documents, answers the question directly, locates the evidence, and selects read of the chunks it ranks highest, one probe long. We evaluate the method as inference, holding the model, the prompt, and the readout fixed and changing only which text reaches each forward pass. On LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025), reading the chunks the map ranks highest, 9k tokens, matches the same models best window read across windows from 32k to 1M tokens and leads embedding, random, and prefix selection at the same budget by 6 to 11 points. Each call caches one probe, so the selected read matches or approaches the best window read with third to fifth of its cache (Figure 1). On InfiniteBench En.MC (Zhang et al., 2024a), with median context of 150k tokens, the same read leads the best window read by 5 points. On BRIGHT (SU et al., 2025) the ranking readout attains the best NDCG@10 and MRR of six methods. Contributions. (1) Factorized reading. decomposition that captures the context of whole text through short, independent local and strided probes, so model with window of tokens reads texts of 2/c tokens without ever reading them at once. (2) The evidence map. The probes answers combine into map of where the evidence sits in the text, at no extra cost. (3) Readouts of the map. The same map ranks documents, answers questions directly, locates the evidence, and selects short read that replaces reading the whole window. 2 Preprint.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Limits of the single long read. Most long-context models fall below quality threshold well before their claimed length, and only half hold up at 32k tokens (Hsieh et al., 2024), the gap widens once the needle shares little vocabulary with the question (Modarressi et al., 2025), content in the middle of long input is used less than content at either end (Liu et al., 2024), and accuracy falls with input length even when retrieval is perfect (Du et al., 2025). The limit these studies share is the pass itself: every token competes with every other for the same decision, and the model is most reliable on the short inputs it reads best. Extending the window. The first response is to make the pass longer. Positional interpolation and its successors extend pretrained window by orders of magnitude with little or no tuning (Chen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024), and keep the quadratic attention and the memory of the original. Sub-quadratic architectures address the cost itself. State-space and linear-attention layers carry fixed-size state (Gu & Dao, 2023; Yang et al., 2025b), and sparse attention reads selected subset of keys (Liu et al., 2025). fixed state alone copies and retrieves from context poorly (Jelassi et al., 2024), so deployed models keep minority of full-attention layers (Lenz et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), whose key-value cache still grows with every token. The largest of these models need multi-GPU node for long read: Jamba-1.5-Large fits 256k context on eight 80GB GPUs with 8-bit expert weights (Jamba Team et al., 2024), and MiniMax-Text-01 was sized to process over 1M tokens on single eight-GPU, 640GB machine with 8-bit quantization (Li et al., 2025). These are also architectures rather than inference methods, trained or continually pretrained with their layers in place, so they do not apply to an existing model. In every case the whole text enters one pass, and the evaluations above find accuracy declining well inside the window. Reading less. The second response keeps the pass short by deciding in advance what enters it. Retrieval-augmented generation reads the top-k chunks retriever selects (Lewis et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020), and prompt compression drops tokens before the pass (Jiang et al., 2023). Dense and late-interaction retrievers (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Khattab & Zaharia, 2020) score passages from representations computed before the query is seen, and such retrievers perform poorly when relevance requires reasoning rather than surface matching (SU et al., 2025). Memory-augmented models retrieve blocks of the readers own key-value cache by similarity, and for EM-LLM also by temporal contiguity (Xiao et al., 2024; Fountas et al., 2025). In every case selection rule fixed before or outside the readers judgment of the answer decides what is read, and what the selector misses cannot be recovered by the read. Language models as judges. The reader can make that decision itself. Pointwise rerankers read relevance score from language models one-word answer, trained (Nogueira et al., 2020) or zero-shot, possibly after generated query and document analyses (Niu et al., 2024), and listwise and setwise rerankers read an ordering (Sun et al., 2023; Zhuang et al., 2024), with the cost per judgment accounted in FLOPs by Peng et al. (2025). judgment read from single answer token is cheap and reliable, but rerankers assume the document fits in one call and that first stage assembled the candidates. Reading in pieces. text that does not fit one call can be judged in parts. FirstP scores the lead passage and MaxP the best passage of document (Dai & Callan, 2019), so every call is bounded, but no call sees beyond its own passage. Chain of Agents processes chunks in sequence, each worker passing generated message to the next and manager writing the answer (Zhang et al., 2024b). LongAgent has members read chunks in parallel and report to leader over several rounds, each round depending on the leaders previous state (Zhao et al., 2024). These systems carry information across the text, but their calls depend on earlier generated outputs, each message is an intermediate that can drop what later chunk would have needed, and the final answer has no stated relation to read of the full text. Bounded, independent calls that still see across the whole text would need different way to cut it. Separable structure and answer-space probing. matrix built from one vector along its rows and one along its columns is the cheapest structure matrix can have, and it is used wherever the full matrix is too costly to measure or learn, from separable filters to low-rank weight updates (Hu et al., 2022). Grid probing carried this structure to inference: it places video frames on KK grid, asks frozen model about each row and each column, and combines the answers into map that selects frames for second pass, 2K calls for 2 frames (Eltahir et al., 2026). Right: the chunks sit on KK grid, here 33, each local probe Li reads consecutive chunks and each strided probe Sj every K-th chunk, and each chunk scores the sum of its two probes. The map peaks at the evidence chunk, and the answer comes from reading the top chunks (Select) or from each options best local and strided scores alone (Direct). with the square root of the number of items rather than with the number itself. long text has no such geometry of its own. If it could be folded into separable grid, the same structure might avoid the two bottlenecks of the single read, the quadratic cost of full attention and the fixed boundary of the window. Together these threads describe what read past the window needs: calls that are bounded and independent, decision made by the reader itself, view of the whole text and not only of its parts, and score that shows where its evidence lies.

sections.title: 3 PERISCOPE
sections.content: Periscope replaces the single forward pass over text with 2K bounded passes and composition rule. The task determines only the answer set of the probe and which readout of the composed scores is used. The model, its serving, and its readout are those of the single read. Nothing is generated, no state passes between calls, and the calls are independent.

sections.title: 3.1 THE PROBE
sections.content: A probe is one forward pass of frozen model θ on span of the text and the question q, read at the first answer token. It returns one score per answer, measuring how strongly the span alone supports that answer. For multiple-choice question with options Y, the prompt lists the options and one more, an abstain option y. The probe score ℓ(y S, q) of each option is its log-odds against abstaining, ℓ(y S, q) = log pθ(y S, q) log pθ(y S, q), (1) where pθ( S, q) is the models probability of each answer at that token. The abstain option lets the model report that the span holds no evidence, so such span scores every option low rather than favoring one at random, and scores from different spans can be compared. For relevance, the question asks whether is relevant to query, and the score is the log-odds of Yes against No.

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: All models are frozen, served with vLLM in bfloat16 on one A100 80GB, and read at single answer token with the settings of Appendix A.1. Every arm runs on the same GPU, so no arm has more memory or compute than another. Every baseline is training-free. Chunks are 500 tokens for question answering and 100 for retrieval.

sections.title: 4.2 BENCHMARKS & BASELINES
sections.content: Question answering uses LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025), 503 four-option questions over contexts of 8k to 2M words in three splits, short (180), medium (215), and long (108), and InfiniteBench En.MC (Zhang et al., 2024a), 229 four-option questions over whole novels with median context of 150k tokens. The models are Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) and the mixture-ofexperts Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (Gemma Team, 2026). The window read reads the longest prefix of the context that fits the window, and we run it at every window the GPU can serve for each model: 32k, 64k, 131k, and 262k natively and 1M with YaRN for the 4B, 131k and 262k for the 27B, and 262k for Gemma. Periscope needs far less: its longest probe is 48k tokens, so it runs at every models native window, without extension. Periscope is run in two ways. Direct answers from the 2K probes alone, with no further call. Select has two stages: the probes build the map, and one more call reads the chunks the map ranks highest, about 9k tokens, and answers. Three baselines replace the map in the second stage and read the same number of chunks: the first K, at random, and the top by cosine similarity to the question under Qwen3-Embedding-4B. Every arm answers every question. Retrieval uses the long-document corpora of BRIGHT (SU et al., 2025), 3,792 documents with medians of 334 to 6,701 tokens by domain and maxima above 1.8 million, and 350 queries stratified sampled across seven of BRIGHT domains, each scored against its whole domain corpus with no candidate pooling. The model is Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025a) at 16k window, and it scores every document with the relevance probe of Section 3.1. Periscope is the ranking readout. The window read has the same model read the longest prefix of each document that fits, as pointwise LLM reranker does (Niu et al., 2024), FirstP reads the first chunk (Dai & Callan, 2019), and BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) and Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the parameter-matched similarity control, are run under the identical protocol. We report NDCG@10, the benchmarks headline metric, MRR, and recall at 1 and 10.

sections.title: 4.4 A SECOND BENCHMARK
sections.content: On InfiniteBench the contexts are whole novels, and two thirds of them exceed the 131k window. The maps read of chunks scores 82.1, 5 points above the best window read, at 262k, and 8 above the read at 131k  (Table 2)  . The gain comes from the novels that do not fit: on the 79 that fit 131k tokens the 131k read is ahead, 82.3 against 78.5, as on the short split of LongBench v2, and on the 150 that do not the maps read leads by 14 points, 84.0 against 70.0. 4.5 IS THE MAP RIGHT? The probe scores must also be right on their own, apart from the read that follows them. Table 3 tests the ranking readout, with no read at all, on BRIGHT, where relevance takes reasoning rather than word overlap. The probes rank the corpora with the best NDCG@10 and MRR of six methods. Against the embedder, retriever trained for the task, the frozen model leads MRR and Recall@1, and trails by half point on Recall@10: the verdict is sharper at the head of the ranking, while similarity fills the top ten more completely. 8 Preprint. sections.content: sc tokens, so on LongBench v2 they process The probes process every token twice in calls of about 2.3 and 2.5 times the tokens of the window read on the short and medium splits and 14 times on the long split. Whether that is more compute than the window read depends on the crossover of Section 3.4, which is 119k tokens for the 4B and 278k for the 27B from their measured coefficients (Figure 3(b), Appendix A.2). Measured on one A100, batch of the 4Bs probes takes 26 at 262k tokens against 40 for the single read, and 108 at 1M against 457 (Figure 3(a)). Memory does not depend on the crossover. At the longest context of the benchmark, 4.5M tokens, one probe of the 27B holds 3.1 GB of cache next to 54 GB of weights, where single read would hold 296 GB, more than three A100s, so the 27B reads it on one GPU. (Figure 1(right)) The 4B served with only 16 GB caches at most 178k tokens in one pass, and its single read ends there while every probe still runs. Past the window, the single read is not available at any price.

sections.title: 5 ABLATIONS
sections.content: We run two ablations with the probes held fixed: what the strided probes add, and how the probes compare with reading in sequence. The strided probes supply the global view. Each local probe sees one neighborhood of the text, and each strided probe sample of all of it, so removing the strided probes isolates what the global view adds (Table 4a). On BRIGHT, reading each chunk alone, as MaxP does, and reading the local spans give the same NDCG@10, .551, so finer local pieces add nothing. Adding the strided probes lifts it to .637. What the local view lacks is not resolution but view of the whole document, and strided probes supply it with that. On LongBench v2 the strided probes add 0.8 on all questions. Independent probes or chain. Chain of Agents (Zhang et al., 2024b), run with the same model, and the same local spans, scores 10 points below the selected read, at three times the latency (Table 4b). Its K+1 calls run in sequence, and each message is written before the next span is read, so what later span would have made relevant may already be gone. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: We asked whether long read can be factorized when it is decision. Periscope reads text through 2K bounded local and strided probes of frozen model, reaching 2/c tokens from window of with the cache of one probe, while achieving comparable performance of full read. Limitations and future work. The method covers decisions over finite answer set. It joins evidence from distant spans only in the selected read, which trails the window read on multi-document QA, and below the crossover it costs more than single read. Two directions follow: readouts for open-ended outputs such as summaries, and distilling the probe scores and maps into retrievers and rankers far cheaper than the model that produced them.

We read the top-20 log-probabilities at the answer position and compute Eq. 1. Thinking mode is disabled where the model has one. Sampling. Temperature 1.0 with top_p= 1, top_k= 1, and min_p= 0. Chunking and grid. Texts are tokenized once and split into c-token chunks.
